name: Discofox offbeat chops
rationale: Short choked downstrokes on every off-beat, sitting between the four-on-the-floor kick like a hi-hat. The busy version adds a light upstroke on the sixteenth after each chop for more drive. Bar 4 lets a chord ring from the 'and' of three (quiet) or pushes a ringing chord on the 'and' of four into the next phrase (busy).

name: Oom-pah with alternating bass
rationale: Classic schlager two-step: a picked bass note on beats 1 and 3 (root, then the fifth string of the shape) and a crisp chord strum on 2 and 4. The busy version fills the 'and' after each chord with an upstroke. Bar 4 walks to a ringing chord on beat 3.

name: Half-note ringing chords
rationale: Big open chords strummed on beats 1 and 3 and left to ring, the warm bed under a slow verse. The busy version keeps the ringing chord on 1 but answers it with driving down-up eighths in the second half of the bar. Bar 4 holds a single whole-bar chord (quiet) or stops after beat 3 for a breath (busy).

name: Driving eighths, accents on 2 and 4
rationale: Straight eighth-note down-up strumming, the sing-along engine of a schlager chorus, with the downstrokes on 2 and 4 played harder and longer than the rest. The quiet version is downstrokes on the beats only, with an upstroke leading into beat 3. Bar 4 pushes a ringing chord onto the last eighth so the new chord arrives early.

name: Bright upstroke skank
rationale: Light upstrokes on every off-beat give a skipping, cheerful lift; the hand rests on the beat. The busy version adds a downstroke on beats 1 and 3 to anchor the bar. Bar 4 ends with a ringing upstroke on the 'and' of four that floats into the next bar.

name: Folk-pop campfire strum
rationale: The down, down-up, up-down-up campfire strum in its schlager-pop form: open, ringing and easy to sing over. The quiet version drops the upstrokes after beat 2 and on the last 'and'. Bar 4 stops on a ringing chord on beat 3.

name: Stop-time with a phrase-end ring
rationale: Firm quarter-note downstrokes cut short, with the whole band 'stopping' on beat 3 of bar 4 and a single big chord ringing out. The busy version adds an upstroke before each beat 3 and doubles beat 4. Made for the last line of a chorus before the title line returns.

name: Foxtrot swing in triplets
rationale: A swung foxtrot feel: downstroke on each beat with a light upstroke on the last triplet before it, like a dancing shuffle. The quiet version keeps only beats 1 and 3 with the swung pickup into 3. Bar 4 lands a long chord on beat 3.

name: Discofox bass note and offbeat chop
rationale: A picked bass note on each beat-one and beat-three, answered by a short chord chop on the following 'and', mirroring the Discofox bass and hi-hat. The busy version chops every 'and' and adds an upstroke on the 'a' of two and four. Bar 4 slides into the next phrase with a string noise and a pushed ringing chord.

name: Sixteenth-note pump on the beat
rationale: A down-up sixteenth pair on every beat ('one-e') that pumps like a dance-floor rhythm guitar, with the rest of each beat muted. The quiet version plays the pair only on beats 2 and 4. Bar 4 ends on a long upstroke from the 'e' of four.

name: Charleston push
rationale: A dotted 'Charleston' figure: a strum on beat 1 and a pushed strum on the 'and' of two, giving a bouncy swing-pop step. The busy version fills beats 3 and 4 with down-up pairs. Bar 4 anticipates the next bar with a ringing chord on the 'and' of four.

name: Whole-note anthem chords
rationale: One ringing downstroke per bar, the most open sound for an intro or a hushed first verse. The busy version strums each beat with a long, even downstroke for a stately sing-along. Bar 4 adds a little picked answer on the top strings (quiet) or a pushed chord on the 'and' of four (busy).

name: Syncopated pop cell
rationale: A three-three-two syncopation (strums on 1, the 'and' of 2, and 4) that gives schlager-pop a modern push. The busy version fills the gaps with upstrokes. Bar 4 turns the cell around and rings from beat 3.

name: Polka-flavoured two-step
rationale: Fast oom-pah in eighths: picked bass on each beat and a short chord chop on every 'and'. The quiet version only chops on the 'and' of two and four. Bar 4 finishes with two firm downstrokes and a stop.

name: Galloping chorus
rationale: A galloping eighth-and-two-sixteenths figure (down, then down-up) on every beat that drives a big uptempo chorus. The quiet version gallops only on beat 1 and rests the hand on the rest of the bar except a downstroke on 3. Bar 4 breaks the gallop into a long chord on beat 3.

name: Anticipated downbeat
rationale: Every bar's chord arrives a sixteenth early, on the last 'a' of the previous bar, and rings across the barline, which gives a lifted, eager feel. The busy version adds chops on beats 2 and 3 and an upstroke before four. Bar 4 waits and lands squarely on beat 1 of the next phrase instead.

name: Schlager ballad: bass, arpeggio, strum
rationale: For slower songs inside the tempo range: a picked bass and a rolling arpeggio of the upper strings on beat 1, then a soft ringing strum on beat 3. The busy version strums on 2 and 4 too, with an upstroke on the 'and' of four. Bar 4 ends with a ringing upstroke.

name: Double-chop offbeats
rationale: Two quick downstroke chops on each off-beat ('and-a'), a punchier Discofox variant that sounds like a doubled hi-hat. The quiet version double-chops only on the 'and' of two and four. Bar 4 replaces the last double chop with a ringing chord on the 'and' of three.

name: Shuffled six-eight chunks
rationale: A six-eight sway written in triplets: a strum on each beat plus the last triplet of beats 2 and 4, like a waltzing folk-pop feel inside four beats. The quiet version uses just beat 1 and beat 3 with ringing chords and the swung pickup into 3. Bar 4 rolls up into the next bar with a triplet upstroke.

name: Big chorus wall
rationale: A wall of full down-up sixteenths on beats 1 and 3 with ringing chords on 2 and 4, the loud 'hands in the air' chorus sound. The quiet version keeps only the ringing chords on 2 and 4 with a pickup upstroke before each. Bar 4 stops dead after beat 2 and leaves space for the singer.

name: Country-schlager boom-chick
rationale: A boom-chick with the bass note on every beat and a short chord chop on the 'and' of each beat, the folk-pop cousin of the oom-pah. The quiet version picks bass on 1 and 3 and chops on the 'and' of 1 and 3 only. Bar 4 ends with a bass walk on the low strings and a ringing chord.

name: Push and stab
rationale: A long ringing chord on beat 1 followed by two dry stabs on the 'and' of three and on four, a call-and-response inside each bar. The busy version adds stabs on the 'and' of one and two. Bar 4 turns the stabs into a pushed ringing chord on the 'and' of four.

name: Upstroke-led reverse strum
rationale: An unusual bright pattern that leads with upstrokes: up on the 'e' before each beat, then down on the beat, so every downstroke has a little flick in front of it. The quiet version does this only into beats 2 and 4. Bar 4 ends on a ringing upstroke from beat 3.

name: Disco sixteenth strut
rationale: A disco-schlager strut: muted downstroke on beat 1, then a sixteenth syncopation on the 'a' of one and the 'e' of three that lets the chord slip off the beat. The busy version keeps the off-beat chops of Discofox on top. Bar 4 uses a fret squeak and a pushed ring on the 'a' of four.

name: Marching quarters with a roll
rationale: Even downstrokes on every beat, slightly short, with a quick down-up-down roll leading into beat 1 of the next bar: the cheerful march of a folk-pop sing-along. The quiet version strums 1 and 3 only and keeps the roll. Bar 4 replaces the roll with a long ring on beat 4.

name: Lazy backbeat ring
rationale: Rest on beat 1 and let a long chord ring from beat 2 to the end of the bar, so the guitar leans on the backbeat while the bass carries beat 1. The busy version answers with upstrokes on the 'and' of three and four. Bar 4 picks a short melodic answer on the top strings instead of strumming beat 4.

name: Pushed two and four
rationale: The backbeat chords are pushed a sixteenth early (the 'a' of one and the 'a' of three) and ring through the beat, a sly syncopation that feels modern but still dances. The busy version adds downstrokes on 1 and 3 and an upstroke after each push. Bar 4 resolves to plain beats and a ringing chord on 3.

name: Triplet roll fills
rationale: Steady quarter downstrokes, with a triplet down-up-down roll on beat 4 that sweeps into the next bar, a showy dance-band touch. The quiet version only rolls in bar 4 and strums beats 1 and 3. Bar 4 in the busy version ends with a long chord after the roll.

name: Verse tick-tock
rationale: A very light verse groove: one short downstroke on beat 1 and an upstroke on the 'and' of two, leaving most of the bar to the voice. The busy version turns it into a skipping down-up pattern across the bar. Bar 4 adds a ringing chord on beat 4.

name: Dotted bounce
rationale: Strums on 1, the 'a' of one and the 'and' of two, then again from beat 3: a dotted, bouncing rhythm that sounds like clapping along. The quiet version plays the figure only in the first half of each bar. Bar 4 stretches the last strum into a ringing chord.

name: Offbeat rings
rationale: Chords strummed on the 'and' of each beat but left ringing instead of choked, a softer, floating version of the Discofox off-beat for gentle verses. The busy version adds short downstrokes on each beat under the rings. Bar 4 holds one long chord from the 'and' of one.

name: Heartbeat pairs
rationale: Down-down pairs on beat 1 and the 'and' of one, then on beat 3 and its 'and', like a heartbeat; a tender schlager-pop pulse. The busy version adds upstrokes on the 'and' of two and four. Bar 4 lets the pair on beat 3 become a ringing chord.

name: Sixteenth strum engine
rationale: Constant down-up sixteenths with accents (longer strums) on the 'and' of every beat, the hand never stops, very energetic for the final chorus. The quiet version plays straight eighth-note downstrokes. Bar 4 stops on beat 3 with a long chord after a squeak.

name: Long upstroke shimmer
rationale: Ringing upstrokes on the 'and' of two and four over a downstroke on beat 1, a glittering, light texture that suits a bright electric. The busy version adds short downstrokes on 2, 3 and 4. Bar 4 picks the top three strings as a small arpeggio after a final shimmer.

name: Half-time bridge
rationale: A half-time feel for bridges and breakdowns: a ringing chord on beat 1 and a single snappy chop on beat 3 of every bar, with the second bar of each pair answering with an upstroke. The busy version doubles the chop on 3 and adds a pickup upstroke. Bar 4 is a long build of quarter strums into the next phrase.

name: Discofox three-chop hook
rationale: A short, catchy chop phrase of three off-beat sixteenths ('and' of one, 'e' of two, 'and' of two) with a long chord on beat 3, a guitar hook that repeats every bar. The quiet version only rings the chord on 3 with one chop before it. Bar 4 answers the hook by moving it to the second half of the bar.

name: Folk-pop triplet sway
rationale: A gentle triplet sway: downstroke on each beat and a light upstroke on the middle triplet of beats 2 and 4, like a folk tune rocking along. The quiet version rings beats 1 and 3 with a middle-triplet upstroke after beat 3. Bar 4 ends with a picked answer on the top strings in triplets.

name: Bass-run turnaround
rationale: Downstrokes on 2 and 4 over a picked root on 1 and 3, and in bar 4 a picked walk up the low strings that leads the ear to the next chord, the dance-band turnaround. The busy version adds upstrokes on the 'and' of two and three. A light slide noise marks the turnaround.

name: Two-bar call and answer
rationale: A two-bar phrase: the first bar is a busy down-up pattern, the second a single ringing chord, so the guitar 'asks' and the singer 'answers'. The quiet version makes the call just three strums. Bar 4 replaces the ringing answer with a stop on beat 2.

name: Final-chorus lift
rationale: Built for the last chorus key-change: downstroke accents on every beat with a sixteenth upstroke after each and a long chord on beat 1, then bar 4 holds back to three big ringing chords that build tension. The quiet version is a ringing chord on 1 and short strums on 3 and its 'and'. Use it where the song lifts.
